>"Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn't, pays it." - 
>Albert Einstein


# Costs Will Double Faster Than You Think

When the City approves a budget, it is not just approving one year of spending.  It is committing the City ***and the taxpayers*** to long-term financial obligations.

Compensation is, by far, the largest recurring commitment in the General Fund.  It includes wages, overtime, retirement contributions, health insurance, payroll taxes, and other employer-paid benefits.

Total compensation commitments grow annually even if no pay raises are given.  This is due to increasing benefit costs.  That means the cost ***compounds over time***.  

Small annual increases lead to large long-term obligations.

---


# Get The Essential Numbers

Before voting on recurring compensation commitments, staff should provide Council with:

1. The fully loaded total compensation for the prior year.  
2. The fully loaded total compensation proposed for the new budget year.  
3. The year-over-year growth rate of total compensation.  
4. The implied doubling time at that growth rate.  
5. A sensitivity range showing what happens if compensation grows at 3%, 4%, 5%, 6%, 4% and 8% annually.

These are not advanced financial tools.  

They are basic measures of structural sustainability.

---

# Why Doubling Time Matters

A growth rate of 5–6% may not sound large.

But at 6% annual growth, total compensation doubles in about 12 years.  
At 5%, it doubles in about 14 years.  
At 4%, it doubles in about 18 years.

Doubling time is not a theory.  It is simple math.

If compensation doubles, the revenue supporting it must also double, which always means increasing tax rates and fees.  Or, services must be reduced (which never happens).

---

# In the End, Council Has the Responsibility

Council members cannot reasonably be expected to reverse-engineer these numbers from hundreds of pages of budget detail.

If the fully loaded compensation growth rate is not clearly presented, then the long-term impact of recurring compensation commitments is ***not transparent***.

The most effective governance requires understanding not only this year's budget, but the rate of growth of large costs over time.

Recurring compensation increases are very long-term commitments.  

They must be matched with long-term, reliable revenue growth.

Without that alignment, significant tax rate and fee increases are inevitable, not optional.

---


# Conclusion

Clear disclosure of total compensation growth and doubling time is super-important for Council to consider each and every year.

It is essential information for making the best decisions.

If Council receives these figures before approving recurring compensation commitments they will make the best decisions possible for the taxpayers.
